content: 1. Laws, policies, and regulations must be established to govern disease notification and the use, security, and confidentiality of collected data. This includes ensuring that patient information is protected and used appropriately. 2. Laboratories conducting HIV diagnostic tests, viral load assessments, and CD4 counts, as well as vital statistics registries, must be integrated into the system where patients are diagnosed or receive care. 3. The organizational structures for disease surveillance should be reviewed, including reporting pathways, processes, forms, data management, and dissemination mechanisms. The potential for utilizing existing systems or building upon them should be assessed, along with estimating the costs of developing or strengthening HIV case surveillance. 4. Data gaps or weaknesses in the HIV case surveillance system must be identified and addressed. This includes determining the data needed for strategic planning, measuring HIV prevalence, and evaluating the effectiveness of the care cascade. 5. Existing HIV patient and program monitoring and reporting systems should be assessed to determine how they can be leveraged for improved surveillance. 6. The feasibility of using electronic medical records, patient registers, and laboratory information systems to transmit data directly to the surveillance program should be evaluated. 7. The interoperability of existing data and information systems, as well as data repositories, must be assessed. Steps should be taken to ensure full interoperability of these systems. 8. The tools and recommendations outlined in the 2017 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance should be adopted and customized to fit the specific context of each country and program. These tools aim to support program improvement, strengthen linkages in the care cascade, and optimize health outcomes. 9. Vital registration systems should be reviewed to evaluate the completeness of death ascertainment, the recording of causes of death, and the accessibility of vital data. 10. Technological capacity, infrastructure, and systems that may facilitate or impede HIV case surveillance should be assessed. 11. The feasibility, costs, barriers, and needs for transitioning from paper-based to electronic systems, including the use of unique patient identifiers, should be evaluated. This includes identifying human resource and training needs, as well as additional infrastructure requirements. 12. Officials responsible for surveillance should be designated at both national and reporting site levels, with oversight from a national surveillance working group. 13. Priority areas for investment in HIV surveillance should be identified. 14. HIV case surveillance should begin with the diagnosis of HIV and build upon existing patient monitoring systems. WHO provides guidance on HIV case definitions. 15. Standardized data collection should include key events such as the first positive HIV test, entry into care, the first CD4 test, initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), viral suppression, and death. For children, additional events include pregnancy in women living with HIV, HIV-exposed infants, infant antiretroviral prophylaxis, and infant polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests. 16. Data on key populations should be routinely collected to describe access to services. However, confidentiality and security are paramount when collecting such data. Patient monitoring records should not include key population categories, and any information collected should support patient management and referral to care rather than program monitoring. 17. The probable route of HIV transmission can be assessed at the point of diagnosis and used to disaggregate data in HIV case surveillance systems. 18. Case report forms must include sufficient information to describe the HIV epidemic by person, place, and time. This includes basic demographic data, facility information, and details related to the sentinel events being reported. WHO provides a model case report form. 19. Surveillance programs must be able to identify and link reports concerning the same individual across multiple sources, preferably using a unique identifier, to create a single, longitudinal case record. WHO provides guidance on such approaches. 20. Key principles for implementing a data management system include ensuring accessibility to authorized personnel, using modifiable software, providing local IT support, maintaining simplicity, linking multiple reports for individual cases, ensuring confidentiality and security, incorporating data quality checks, and supporting data transfer between subnational and national levels. The system must comply with national laws and policies governing public health data and ensure compatibility with standardized data collection tools. 21. Countries should invest in robust and secure data systems and strengthen the interoperability of electronic databases. Open-source standards for data systems should be adopted. WHO recommends allocating 5–10% of program budgets to strengthen monitoring and evaluation. 22. Case surveillance systems must be routinely monitored and comprehensively evaluated at least annually (ideally every six months) to ensure effective surveillance processes and high-quality data. 23. Countries should assess and differentiate the security of data elements and invest in robust databases, laws, and policies to protect data security and confidentiality based on risks and benefits in individual settings. 24. Countries should progressively transition from paper-based to electronic patient information systems, particularly in facilities with more than 2,000 patients. WHO provides an example of a tiered approach for this transition. 25. HIV case surveillance data must describe the sociodemographic characteristics and risk factors that identify modes of transmission, geographical distribution, and changes over time. These data can strengthen prevention and treatment activities in areas with high case diagnoses and identify where the HIV epidemic is concentrated. 26. Surveillance data may be combined with other information on the HIV epidemic, including program monitoring data, qualitative studies, vital statistics, censuses, sexually transmitted infection data, and surveys, to account for changes in the epidemic. 27. Analytical techniques such as triangulation, data synthesis, and second-generation surveillance can be employed to correlate surveillance data with other data sources. 28. HIV case surveillance systems collect longitudinal data on individuals, providing opportunities to analyze HIV care cascade indicators, investigate gaps, and address them effectively.
